title: When the Board Fires the Founder

parts.visual:
A founder builds a company from zero to $50 Million in revenue. They are brilliant at building product, but terrible at managing 500 employees. The company is in chaos. During a board meeting, the VC and the Independent Director vote to remove the founder from the CEO position. The founder is escorted out of their own building by security.

The Ousting:
1. The Transition: Most visionary founders are great at '0 to 1' (inventing), but terrible at '1 to 100' (corporate management). Boards routinely fire the visionary founder to bring in a boring, professional 'Suit' CEO.
2. The Math: It is not a conspiracy; it is just math. If the founders control 2 board seats, and the external investors/independents control 3 board seats, the founders can be fired at any moment by a simple majority vote.
parts.audio: Steve Jobs was fired from Apple. Travis Kalanick was fired from Uber. Noah Glass was fired from Twitter. If you lose control of your board seats, your company is no longer your company. You serve at the pleasure of the Board.

questions.question: Why do Boards usually replace the original Founder/CEO right before the company goes public (IPO)?
options: Wall Street demands predictability. Public markets hate volatile, aggressive visionary founders. They want a calm, predictable, experienced executive who has managed a public company before. The board fires the founder to please Wall Street.
questions.correct_answer: Wall Street demands predictability. Public markets hate volatile, aggressive visionary founders. They want a calm, predictable, experienced executive who has managed a public company before. The board fires the founder to please Wall Street.
questions.explanation: The skills to start a company are the opposite of the skills to run a public one.

questions.question: Listen to the VC explaining how a firing happens. What is the tactical move?
questions.tts_text: We don't want a messy public fight that destroys the stock price. We privately offer the founder a new, fake title called 'Chief Innovation Officer' or 'Chairman of the Board'. It lets them save face publicly, while secretly stripping them of all power.
options: The 'Kick Upstairs'. A brutal corporate maneuver. To avoid bad PR and employee panic, the board promotes the founder to a highly prestigious-sounding role that actually has zero operational control, while the new CEO takes over the real power.
They give them a new car.
questions.correct_answer: The 'Kick Upstairs'. A brutal corporate maneuver. To avoid bad PR and employee panic, the board promotes the founder to a highly prestigious-sounding role that actually has zero operational control, while the new CEO takes over the real power.
questions.explanation: A golden parachute and an empty throne.

questions.question: If a founder is fired as CEO, what happens to the stock they own?
options: If they have fully vested their stock (e.g., worked for 4 years), they keep all of it. They are no longer the CEO, but they are still a massive shareholder. If the new CEO succeeds and the company is sold, the fired founder still becomes a billionaire.
questions.correct_answer: If they have fully vested their stock (e.g., worked for 4 years), they keep all of it. They are no longer the CEO, but they are still a massive shareholder. If the new CEO succeeds and the company is sold, the fired founder still becomes a billionaire.
questions.explanation: You lose the job, but you keep your vested ownership.

questions.question: How did Mark Zuckerberg make it completely, mathematically impossible for his board to ever fire him?
options: He is very nice to them.

He structured the company with 'Dual-Class' voting shares. His specific shares count for 10 votes each. Even though he only owns a small percentage of the company's financial value, he controls 60% of the voting power. He is legally un-fireable.

questions.explanation: The ultimate defense is controlling the voting math.

pairs.match: Giving a fired founder a fake title like 'Chairman' to avoid bad PR
Super-voting shares that make a founder mathematically un-fireable
A visionary who is great at inventing but terrible at corporate management
The stock you get to keep even after the board fires you
